title: Family Separation 2.0: Infants Taken at Border Under Noem
description_short: Family Separation 2.0: Infants Taken at Border Under Noem
description_medium: In early 2025, the Trump administration under DHS Secretary Kristi Noem revived family separation policies at the southern border. Reports emerged of infants and toddlers being separated from parents in immigration custody. Unlike the 2018 policy, the new approach was implemented without a formal public announcement. Child welfare advocates documented cases of children as young as several months old held separately from parents. The administration denied it was policy while individual cases continued emerging from detention facilities along the Texas and Arizona borders.
description_long:
Reports in early 2025 described infants and toddlers being separated from parents in immigration custody under DHS Secretary Kristi Noem. Child-welfare advocates said they had documented children only several months old held apart from parents at facilities near the Texas and Arizona borders. The administration denied that family separation was its policy, while accounts of individual cases continued to emerge.

The distinction between a formally announced program and reported custody practices is central to the dispute. The absence of a public policy announcement does not resolve what happened to particular families, while reports of individual cases do not establish a uniform national rule. The incidents raised immediate concerns about the treatment and welfare of very young children in detention.

Reports and advocacy accounts identify individual cases, but do not establish how many families were separated or define a nationwide practice. The accounts also do not resolve the legal outcome of each case. The event concerns the reported separations and the conflict between those descriptions and the administration's denial.
